newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall on interest rate fears in year's lowest volume.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall on interest rate fears in year's lowest volume.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell sharply in the slowest trading session of the year Friday after unexpectedly strong data reinforced fears that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates to head off inflation as the economy continues to grow.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 31.44 points at 5,616.21 after being down nearly 60 points early in the day.
For the week, the index lost 106.53 points, its worst loss since the last week of May, when it dropped nearly 120 points, just days after climbing to a record close of 5,778 on May 22.
The trading volume of 256 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange eclipsed the previous low of 281.3 million set July 29. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,469 to 802.
The sell-off was sparked by strong July factory orders and a stunning jump in the August Chicago Purchasing Managers Index.
"The Chicago PMI number today was very ugly," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "That seemed to be the catalyst."

The Chicago index, which jumped to an almost unheard of 60.0 from 51.2 in July, sparked a nearly full point fall in the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond, sending the yield to 7.12 percent, nearly a seven-week high, up from Thursday's 7.04 percent.

The regional index, when coupled with Thursday's large upward revision of gross domestic product and surging home sales data, shook markets that had largely dismissed the possibility of an interest rate rise before the November elections.
The July factory orders report showed a 1.8 percent increase in orders, nearly double the rate of growth economists had expected.
"Until these last reports, almost no one thought the evidence would be that overwhelming," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisors.
Although cyclical and smaller-cap stocks outperformed the rest of the market, analysts attributed that to the companies' heightened reliance on the nation's economic cycles.
Analysts said that while the trading activity may recover after Labour Day, market jitters are likely to persist.
"Next week should be a much better test for volume, but the market is still one day bullish and one day bearish," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio manager at Smith Barney.
"Until they can figure out what's going on (in the economy), I don't see that being resolved quickly," he said.

Financial stocks continued to feel the weight of renewed interest rate worries, with Citicorp falling 1-3/4 to 83-1/4, BankAmerica Corp. off 1-1/4 to 77-1/2 and Chase Manhattan Corp. down 1-1/2 to 74-3/8.
However, Boatmen's Bancshares surged 10-5/16 to 53-1/4, after it agreed to be acquired by NationsBank Corp. for about $9.5 billion.
NationsBank, which will swap about 0.65 of a share for each Boatmen's share, slid 7-1/4 to 85-1/8, as some analysts reckoned it was paying too high a price.

ValuJet Inc. jumped 1-1/2 to 12-1/2 after winning tentative approval from the Federal Aviation Administration to resume operations. Company officials said the low-cost carrier could be flying again in a week.

Delta Air Lines fell 1-1/4 to 70-7/8 and AMR Corp., which owns American Airlines, fell 2-1/2 to 82. Both are regional competitors of ValuJet, although rising interest rates also likely played a role in the declines.
PepsiCo rebounded slightly from recent selling pressure, rising 1/4 to 28-7/8.
Dell Computer Corp. gained 1/2 to 67-1/8 after being selected to fill a vacancy in the S&P 500 index of companies.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 3.53 points to 1,141.50.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 5.41 to 651.99. The American Stock Exchange index was off 1.66 to 559.68.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 2.37 to 350.99. The average share was down 26 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,434.026, down 40.244 or 0.62 percent.
